Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room
Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: Threat items imply an ongoing personal-danger/being-followed formulation, which is hard to reconcile with trauma to a loved one; they read more like direct interpersonal victimization than fear for a loved one.

Within Threat, 'Checking Behind' and 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' reflect hypervigilant danger avoidance, while 'Risky Behavior' points in the opposite direction behaviorally; this combination is possible but clinically strained without any other items supporting disinhibition.

Memory item 'Pain Recall' implies bodily re-experiencing of injury to the patient's own body, which is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one unless she was also directly harmed; the other memory items do not suggest that.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, a prominent risky-behavior item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by fear/avoidance and reliving rather than self-endangering behavior. It pulls the threat profile in a different direction without support from other nodes.

issues.item: Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall in the same body parts as during the event implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma. That is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one, especially given no other items indicate direct physical victimization.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: The body-focused negative appraisals suggest distrust of one's own injured or trauma-reactive body, which fits direct bodily trauma better than trauma centered on harm to a loved one. In this profile they are not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, 'military topics' is hard to justify unless the loved one’s trauma was specifically military-related; that context is not represented anywhere else in the profile, so this trigger appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room
issues.explanation: 'Locked spaces' suggests a confinement/entrapment trauma context, but the rest of the profile centers on reliving, terror, and generalized danger after trauma to a loved one rather than a personal entrapment event. Without corroborating memory or appraisal content, this trigger looks clinically out of place.

vignette: The afternoon Leila’s brother died began like any other desert hike, until the narrow canyon walls suddenly groaned. She had been standing on a flat stretch of shale when a section of the ridge gave way, sending a wall of dirt and boulders cascading into the wash. He had stumbled back against the rock face, his boots scraping helplessly against the stone, just inches from the churning water below. She watched him press his palms flat against the cold rock, his mouth opening in a silent plea before the current caught his jacket and pulled him under. The smell of wet earth, the grinding of stone, and the terrifying finality of his grip leaving her hands are imprinted on her the way a scar is imprinted on skin. In the weeks that followed, Leila found that the canyon never left her. When the memory came back, it felt completely real across all her senses at once: the grit in her teeth, the damp chill on her neck, the crushing weight of the air. Remembering the event brought back the same terror she felt at the time, and something in her surroundings could instantly bring back the full memory without warning—a sudden draft, the sound of distant traffic, the shadow of a tree line. Her body kept reacting as if she were still in that wash, heart hammering, breath shortening, even when she was safe in her apartment. She had come to believe that her own pulse was a traitor. On guard at all times, she scanned every room before stepping inside, her neck tense, her eyes tracking exits. Sleep eluded her. Nerves remained stretched tight, certain that if she let her watchfulness drop, the ground would give way beneath her again. The patterns that formed were slow and total. She avoided going to unfamiliar places because she could not assess the danger, declining client site visits that had once been routine for her work as an auditor. When she did have to inspect a client’s secure records room, however, the heavy door clicked shut behind her, and the locked space instantly mirrored the narrow rock crevice that had held her brother. The walls seemed to close in, the air grew thin, and she had to back out, leaving the clipboard untouched. She stopped hiking, stopped driving near open canyons, and flinched at news reports detailing drownings or collapses, each reminder of victims making her chest tighten until she had to step outside. Driving past a stretch of scrubland that resembled the canyon, she would pull over and sit with the engine running, unable to move until the sensation passed. Over months, she had lost her faith in people, in life, in a higher power that would let a sudden slide take someone so quickly. She could not stop bad things from happening to me, she told herself when reviewing audit reports late at night, her eyes burning. The world felt fundamentally unpredictable, and her work shifted as she declined travel, took longer on routine file checks, and quietly withdrew from colleagues who asked about her fatigue. Her calendar, once packed with regional office tours, now showed only virtual calls and a single, familiar desk. Leila finally booked an intake after a Tuesday evening when a routine inventory walk at her office triggered a full reliving that left her shaking against a filing cabinet for twenty minutes. What frightened her most was the certainty that the panic would never quiet, that the terror would keep hijacking her days and her nights until she had nowhere left to work or live. She is hoping to find a way to sleep through the night, to stop bracing for a disaster that has already passed, and to return to the audit trails she once managed without her hands trembling. She does not ask for the memories to vanish, only for her body to believe, finally, that she is no longer standing in the wash.
